Submissions of workman:- 

10. While arguing the case, AR for workman contended that in this case, workman was appointed by 
respondent 10.1 under a camouflage agreement with respondent 10.2. The workman was appointed directly by 
respondent 10.1 on 17.10.2016 as sweeper and his services were dispensed with on 27.10.2018 without any 
reason in violation of Section 25F, 25G and 25H of the Act as no compensation was paid to the workman and 
junior to him were retained in service and fresh appointment were made after termination of the workman. So 
far as the agreements between the respondent no.1 & 2 are concerned, they are totally not tenable and is unfair 
labour practice. The work performed by the workman is of perennial in nature. The contractor was not having 
any license. The contractor has left after three months. No domestic inquiry was held before terminating the 
service of the workman, which is mandatory under the Act. 


Submissions of respondent no.1:- 

11. On the other hand, AR for respondent 10.1 contended that the workman was engaged by respondent 
no.2 (contractor) as per agreement executed between respondent 10.1 & 2 on outsource basis and there is no 
relationship of employer and employee between respondent 10.1 and the workman. Wages were paid by the 
respondent 10.2 to the workman and there was no role of respondent 10.1 in appointing or terminating the 
services of the workman. Workman is employee of respondent 10.2. If there is any violation of provision of 
the Act, then it is done by respondent no.2. As per Ex.R3, all dues were paid by the contractor with regard to 
EPF and ESI etc. The workman and other safai karamcharis formed union in the Headquarter, which is not 
permitted as per Ex.R4. Respondent 10.1 being the Government Agency, workman is trying to take benefit of 
his appointment by respondent no.2 and has filed a false claim after concealing material facts and claim of the 
workman is not maintainable. 


12. Ihave given due consideration to the arguments advanced by AR for both the parties. 
Findings:- 
13. The first contention regarding the applicant is that whether applicant comes within the definition of 


workman as is defined in Section 2(s) of the Act. I may mention that applicant was appointed as sweeper as 
per his claim petition and affidavit submitted before the Tribunal. In plain words the applicant was performing 
his duties as labourer/unskilled worker. He was not in supervisory or administrative post requiring him to 
perform only administrative duties. While interpreting Section 2(s) Hon’ble Supreme Court in the case of 
Devinder Singh Vs. Municipal Council, Sanaur, AIR 2011 Supreme Court 2532,has observed as follows:- 
“The source of employment, the quantum of recruitment, the terms & conditions of 
employment/ contract of service, the quantum of wages/ pay and mode of payment are 
not at all relevant for deciding whether or not a person is a workman within the 
meaning of Section 2(s) of the Act. The definition of workman also does not make any 
distinction between full time and part time employee or a person appointed on contract 
basis. There is nothing in the plain language of Section 2(s) from which it can be 
inferred that only person employed on regular basis or a person employed for doing 
whole time job is a workman and the one employed on temporary, part time or contract 
basis on fixed wages or as a casual employee or for doing duty for fixed hours is not a 
workman.” 
14. Thus Hon’ble Supreme Court has clarified that the definition of workman also does not make any 
distinction between full time or part time employee or a person appointed on contract basis. There is nothing in 
plain language of Section 2(s) from which it can be infer that only person employed on regular basis or a 
person employed for doing whole time job is a workman and the one employed on temporary, part time or 
contract basis on fixed wages or as a casual employee or for doing duty for fixed hours is not a workman. In 
view of the ratio of law enunciated in the above ruling, in my considered opinion the applicant herein 
admittedly falls within the definition of ‘workman’ under Section 2(s) of the Act. 
15. The Hon’ble Supreme Court after analyzing the catena of cases has laid down in Balwant Raj 
Saluja Vs. Air India Limited in Civil Appeal No.10266 dated 25.08.2014, two well recognized tests to find 
out whether the labours are the contract employees of the principal employer are:- 
1) Whether the principal employer pays the salary instead of contractor and 
2) Whether the principal employer controls and supervise the work of the employees? 
16. The facts regarding the payment of salary by the management or contractor has not been stated in 
the claim petition of the workman. In fact, claim petition is totally silent regarding the payment of wages, 
salary, letter of appointment by respondent no.1 or by contractor or anything likewise. Thus, this basic feature 
for holding the relationship of employer and employee i.e. between respondent 10.1 and workman totally 
lacking not in the pleading but also in the evidence submitted by the workman.However, MW1 Colonel 
K P Singh in his cross examination has stated that it is responsibility of the contractor to pay monthly wages to 
the conservancy staff provided by him. Respondent 10.1 has nothing to do with the minimum wages, DC rate 
to the conservancy staff. Contractor is responsible to give notice to the conservancy staff provided by him. 
Respondent no.1 has no roll in terminating the services of the workman. Thus, it was the respondent no.2 who 
was required to ensure the payment of wages to the workers engaged by him from time to time.

17. It is also added here that respondent 10.1 has also placed on record documents Ex.R-1 to Ex.R-4. 
Ex.R-2 is the contract agreement between respondent 10.1 & 2. Thus, from the adduced evidence, it emerges 
that workman was paid salary by the contractor and he was being controlled and supervised by the contractor. 
Thus, there does not exist any relationship of employee and employer between the workman and respondent 
10.1. However, there exists relation of employee and employer between the workman and respondent 10.2. 


18. It is also added here that as per definition of contractor as given in the Section 2(c) of the Contract 
Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970 (hereinafter called as Contract Act), respondent no.2 was 
supplying contract labour to the respondent 10.1. Thus, respondent no.2 would fall under the definition of 
contractor. Section 2(c) of the Contract Act is reproduced as under: 


“Contractor”, in relation to an establishment, means a person who undertakes to 
produce a given result for the establishment, other than a mere supply of goods or 
articles of manufacture to such establishment, through contract labour or who supplies 
contract labour for any work of the establishment and includes a sub-contractor; 


19. TheHon’ble Apex Court in the case of Banglore Water Supply & Sewerage Board Vs. A. Rajappa 
1978(36) FLR 266 dealt at length with the ambit and scope of expression “industry” as defined in Section 20) 
of the Act, and has laid down triple test for determining whether a particular establishment is industry or not. 
The triple test is where (a) systematic activity (b) organized by cooperation between employer and employee 
(the direct and substantial element is commercial (c) for the production or distribution of goods and services to 
calculated to satisfy human wants and wishes prima facie is an “Industry” in that enterprise. The workman was 
doing work i.e. systematic activity for respondent 10.1 at the asking of respondent 10.2 and there was 
cooperation between the workman and respondent no.2, which involve substantial commercial element for 
rendering service to satisfy human wants. Thus, respondent no.2 would be termed as industry. 


20. Workman in his deposition has clearly stated that there was non-compliance of Section 25F, 25G 
and 25H of the Act. He also stated that he was appointed on 17.10.2016 and he was paid minimum wages 
prescribed by Central Government and was working with respondent 10.1. He was not given any 
compensation before terminating his services on 27.10.2018. In his cross examination, he has further stated 
that his salary used to be credited in his bank account. But he has not placed on record any bank account, in 
which his salary was credited in order to enable this Court to see who was making payment to the workman. 
However, there is no denial that the workman was paid salary by respondent no.2 (contractor). However, from 
the agreement dated 05.07.2018 (Ex.R-2) placed on file by respondent no.1, it emerges that safai karamcharis 
were provided by respondent no.2 (contractor) to work with respondent no.1. Thus, workman was employee of 
respondent 10.2 and not of respondent 10.1 as has been discussed above. There does not exist any relationship 
of employee and employer between the workman and respondent 10.1. However, there exists relation of 
employee and employer between the workman and respondent 10.2. 


21. Admittedly, there is non-compliance of Section 25F of the Act by respondent no.2. However, as 
regards violation of other provisions i.e. Section 25G and 25H of the Act, there is no evidence lead by the 
workman. Hence, workman is entitled for compensation from respondent no.2. 


22. It is also added here that there is no iota of evidence that any unfair labour practice used by 
respondent 10.1 by entering into contract with contractors for supply of safai karamcharis and agreement 
executed between respondent 10.1 and 2 cannot be said to be any unfair labour practice. So far as contentions 
of AR for workman that the work performed by the workman is of perennial in nature and no domestic inquiry 
was held before terminating the services of workman are concerned, in this regard, it is pointed out that 
workman was entitled only for compensation under Section 25F of the Act by respondent no.2 (contractor) and 
no domestic inquiry was required to be conducted. Merely because work is of perennial in nature does not 
mean that any right has accrued in favour of the workman to get employment with respondent no.1, which is a 
department of Civil Defence run by Government of India and for that regular recruitment procedure is 
provided. Workman cannot seek backdoor entry into service. Moreover, workman is not employee of 
respondent 10.1 being employee of respondent 10.2 (contractor). 


23. In view of above discussion, it is held that since respondent no.2 (contractor) is currently not 
working with respondent no.1, so keeping in view the tenure of service rendered by the workman and salary 
given to him during the period of his stay with the contractor and non-compliance of Section 25F of the Act, 
this Tribunal is of the considered opinion that workman is entitled for compensation. 


24. Keeping in view the fact and circumstances of the present case, the following scheme of 
compensation is deemed fit by this Tribunal: 


Workman who worked for less than 2 years with contractor shall be entitled for Rs.20,000/-.

25. Present workman employed on 17.10.2016 and was terminated on 27.10.2018 (more than 2 years 
and less than 5 years), so he is entitled for Rs.30,000/-. 


26. Respondent no.2 is directed to pay the workman Rs.30,000/- within one month from the date of the

2) Whether the principal employer controls and supervise the work of the employees? 


16. The facts regarding the payment of salary by the management or contractor has not been stated in the claim 
petition of the workman. In fact, claim petition is totally silent regarding the payment of wages, salary, letter of 
appointment by respondent 10.1 or by contractor or anything likewise. Thus, this basic feature for holding the 
relationship of employer and employee i.e. between respondent 10.1 and workman totally lacking not in the pleading 
but also in the evidence submitted by the workman.However, MW1 Colonel K P Singh in his cross examination has 
stated that it is responsibility of the contractor to pay monthly wages to the conservancy staff provided by him. 
Respondent 10.1 has nothing to do with the minimum wages, DC rate to the conservancy staff. Contractor is 
responsible to give notice to the conservancy staff provided by him. Respondent 10.1 has no roll in terminating the 
services of the workman. Thus, it was the respondent no.2 who was required to ensure the payment of wages to the 
workers engaged by him from time to time.

17. It is also added here that respondent 10.1 has also placed on record documents Ex.R-1 to Ex.R-4. Ex.R-2 is 
the contract agreement between respondent no.1 & 2. Thus, from the adduced evidence, it emerges that workman was 
paid salary by the contractor and he was being controlled and supervised by the contractor. Thus, there does not exist 
any relationship of employee and employer between the workman and respondent 10.1. However, there exists relation 
of employee and employer between the workman and respondent no.2. 


18. It is also added here that as per definition of contractor as given in the Section 2(c) of the Contract Labour 
(Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970 (hereinafter called as Contract Act), respondent no.2 was supplying contract 
labour to the respondent no.1. Thus, respondent no.2 would fall under the definition of contractor. Section 2(c) of the 
Contract Act is reproduced as under: 


“Contractor”, in relation to an establishment, means a person who undertakes to produce a given result for the 
establishment, other than a mere supply of goods or articles of manufacture to such establishment, through contract 
labour or who supplies contract labour for any work of the establishment and includes a sub-contractor; 


19. TheHon’ble Apex Court in the case of Banglore Water Supply & Sewerage Board Vs. A. Rajappa 1978(36) 
FLR 266 dealt at length with the ambit and scope of expression “industry” as defined in Section 2(j) of the Act, and 


has laid down triple test for determining whether a particular establishment is industry or not. The triple test is where 
(a) systematic activity (b) organized by cooperation between employer and employee (the direct and substantial 
element is commercial (c) for the production or distribution of goods and services to calculated to satisfy human 
wants and wishes prima facie is an “Industry” in that enterprise. The workman was doing work i.e. systematic activity 
for respondent 10.1 at the asking of respondent 10.2 and there was cooperation between the workman and respondent 
no.2, which involve substantial commercial element for rendering service to satisfy human wants. Thus, respondent 
no.2 would be termed as industry. 


20. Workman in his deposition has clearly stated that there was non-compliance of Section 25F, 25G and 25H of 
the Act. He also stated that he was appointed on 01.04.2013 and he was paid minimum wages prescribed by Central 
Government and was working with respondent 10.1. He was not given any compensation before terminating his 
services on 27.10.2018. In his cross examination, he has further stated that his salary used to be credited in his bank 
account. But he has not placed on record any bank account, in which his salary was credited in order to enable this 
Court to see who was making payment to the workman. However, there is no denial that the workman was paid salary 
by respondent no.2 (contractor). However, from the agreement dated 05.07.2018 (Ex.R-2) placed on file by 
respondent 10.1, it emerges that safai karamchari were provided by respondent no.2 (contractor) to work with 
respondent no.1. Thus, workman was employee of respondent no.2 and not of respondent no.1 as has been discussed 
above. There does not exist any relationship of employee and employer between the workman and respondent no.1. 
However, there exists relation of employee and employer between the workman and respondent 10.2. 


21. Admittedly, there is non-compliance of Section 25F of the Act by respondent no.2. However, as regards 
violation of other provisions i.e. Section 25G and 25H of the Act, there is no evidence lead by the workman. Hence, 
workman is entitled for compensation from respondent no.2. 


22. It is also added here that there is no iota of evidence that any unfair labour practice used by respondent no.1 
by entering into contract with contractors for supply of safai karamchari and agreement executed between respondent 
10.1 and 2 cannot be said to be any unfair labour practice. So far as contentions of AR for workman that the work 
performed by the workman is of perennial in nature and no domestic inquiry was held before terminating the services 
of workman are concerned, in this regard, it is pointed out that workman was entitled only for compensation under 
Section 25F of the Act by respondent no.2 (contractor) and no domestic inquiry was required to be conducted. Merely 
because work is of perennial in nature does not mean that any right has accrued in favour of the workman to get 
employment with respondent no.1, which is a department of Civil Defence run by Government of India and for that 
regular recruitment procedure is provided. Workman cannot seek backdoor entry into service. Moreover, workman is 
not employee of respondent 10.1 being employee of respondent no.2 (contractor). 


23. In view of above discussion, it is held that since respondent no.2 (contractor) is currently not working with 
respondent 10.1, so keeping in view the tenure of service rendered by the workman and salary given to him during the 
period of his stay with the contractor and non-compliance of Section 25F of the Act, this Tribunal is of the considered 
opinion that workman is entitled for compensation.

deemed fit by this Tribunal:

13. The first contention regarding the applicant is that whether applicant comes within the definition of 
workman as is defined in Section 2(s) of the Act. I may mention that applicant was appointed as sweeper as per his 
claim petition and affidavit submitted before the Tribunal. In plain words the applicant was performing his duties as 
labourer/unskilled worker. She was not in supervisory or administrative post requiring him to perform only 
administrative duties. While interpreting Section 2(s) Hon’ble Supreme Court in the case of Devinder Singh Vs. 
Municipal Council, Sanaur, AIR 2011 Supreme Court 2532,has observed as follows:- 


“The source of employment, the quantum of recruitment, the terms & conditions of employment/ contract of 
service, the quantum of wages/ pay and mode of payment are not at all relevant for deciding whether or not a 
person is a workman within the meaning of Section 2(s) of the Act. The definition of workman also does not 
make any distinction between full time and part time employee or a person appointed on contract basis. 
There is nothing in the plain language of Section 2(s) from which it can be inferred that only person 
employed on regular basis or a person employed for doing whole time job is a workman and the one 
employed on temporary, part time or contract basis on fixed wages or as a casual employee or for doing duty 
for fixed hours is not a workman.” 


14. Thus Hon’ble Supreme Court has clarified that the definition of workman also does not make any distinction 
between full time or part time employee or a person appointed on contract basis. There is nothing in plain language of 
Section 2(s) from which it can be infer that only person employed on regular basis or a person employed for doing 
whole time job is a workman and the one employed on temporary, part time or contract basis on fixed wages or as a 
casual employee or for doing duty for fixed hours is not a workman. In view of the ratio of law enunciated in the 
above ruling, in my considered opinion the applicant herein admittedly falls within the definition of ‘workman’ under 
Section 2(s) of the Act. 


15. The Hon’ble Supreme Court after analyzing the catena of cases has laid down in Balwant Raj Saluja Vs. Air 
India Limited in Civil Appeal No.10266 dated 25.08.2014, two well recognized tests to find out whether the labours 
are the contract employees of the principal employer are:- 


1) Whether the principal employer pays the salary instead of contractor and 
2) Whether the principal employer controls and supervise the work of the employees?

appointment by respondent 10.1 or by contractor or anything likewise. Thus, this basic feature for holding the 
relationship of employer and employee i.e. between respondent 10.1 and workman totally lacking not in the pleading 
but also in the evidence submitted by the workman. However, MW1 Colonel K P Singh in his cross examination has

Findings:- 

13. The first contention regarding the applicant is that whether applicant comes within the definition of 
workman as is defined in Section 2(s) of the Act. I may mention that applicant was appointed as sweeper as per his 
claim petition and affidavit submitted before the Tribunal. In plain words the applicant was performing his duties as 
labourer/unskilled worker. He was not in supervisory or administrative post requiring him to perform only 
administrative duties. While interpreting Section 2(s) Hon’ble Supreme Court in the case of Devinder Singh Vs. 
Municipal Council, Sanaur, AIR 2011 Supreme Court 2532,has observed as follows:- 


“The source of employment, the quantum of recruitment, the terms & conditions of employment contract of 
service, the quantum of wages/ pay and mode of payment are not at all relevant for deciding whether or not a 
person is a workman within the meaning of Section 2(s) of the Act. The definition of workman also does not 
make any distinction between full time and part time employee or a person appointed on contract basis. 
There is nothing in the plain language of Section 2(s) from which it can be inferred that only person 
employed on regular basis or a person employed for doing whole time job is a workman and the one 
employed on temporary, part time or contract basis on fixed wages or as a casual employee or for doing duty 
for fixed hours is not a workman.” 


14. Thus Hon’ble Supreme Court has clarified that the definition of workman also does not make any distinction 
between full time or part time employee or a person appointed on contract basis. There is nothing in plain language of 
Section 2(s) from which it can be infer that only person employed on regular basis or a person employed for doing 
whole time job is a workman and the one employed on temporary, part time or contract basis on fixed wages or as a 
casual employee or for doing duty for fixed hours is not a workman. In view of the ratio of law enunciated in the 
above ruling, in my considered opinion the applicant herein admittedly falls within the definition of ‘workman’ under 
Section 2(s) of the Act. 


15. The Hon’ble Supreme Court after analyzing the catena of cases has laid down in Balwant Raj Saluja Vs. Air 
India Limited in Civil Appeal No.10266 dated 25.08.2014, two well recognized tests to find out whether the labours 
are the contract employees of the principal employer are:- 


1) Whether the principal employer pays the salary instead of contractor and 
2) Whether the principal employer controls and supervise the work of the employees? 


16. The facts regarding the payment of salary by the management or contractor has not been stated in the claim 
petition of the workman. In fact, claim petition is totally silent regarding the payment of wages, salary, letter of 
appointment by respondent 10.1 or by contractor or anything likewise. Thus, this basic feature for holding the 
relationship of employer and employee i.e. between respondent no.1 and workman totally lacking not in the pleading 
but also in the evidence submitted by the workman.However, MW1 Colonel K P Singh in his cross examination has 
stated that it is responsibility of the contractor to pay monthly wages to the conservancy staff provided by him. 
Respondent 10.1 has nothing to do with the minimum wages, DC rate to the conservancy staff. Contractor is 
responsible to give notice to the conservancy staff provided by him. Respondent 10.1 has no roll in terminating the 
services of the workman. Thus, it was the respondent no.2 who was required to ensure the payment of wages to the 
workers engaged by him from time to time. 


17. It is also added here that respondent no.1 has also placed on record documents Ex.R-1 to Ex.R-4. Ex.R-2 is 
the contract agreement between respondent no.1 & 2. Thus, from the adduced evidence, it emerges that workman was 
paid salary by the contractor and he was being controlled and supervised by the contractor. Thus, there does not exist 
any relationship of employee and employer between the workman and respondent 10.1. However, there exists relation 
of employee and employer between the workman and respondent no.2. 


18. It is also added here that as per definition of contractor as given in the Section 2(c) of the Contract Labour 
(Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970 (hereinafter called as Contract Act), respondent no.2 was supplying contract 
labour to the respondent 10.1. Thus, respondent no.2 would fall under the definition of contractor. Section 2(c) of the 
Contract Act is reproduced as under: 


“Contractor”, in relation to an establishment, means a person who undertakes to produce a given result for the 
establishment, other than a mere supply of goods or articles of manufacture to such establishment, through 
contract labour or who supplies contract labour for any work of the establishment and includes a sub- 
contractor;

19. TheHon’ble Apex Court in the case of Banglore Water Supply & Sewerage Board Vs. A. Rajappa 1978(36) 


FLR 266 dealt at length with the ambit and scope of expression “industry” as defined in Section 2(j) of the Act, and 
has laid down triple test for determining whether a particular establishment is industry or not. The triple test is where 
(a) systematic activity (b) organized by cooperation between employer and employee (the direct and substantial 
element is commercial (c) for the production or distribution of goods and services to calculated to satisfy human 
wants and wishes prima facie is an “Industry” in that enterprise. The workman was doing work i.e. systematic activity 
for respondent 10.1 at the asking of respondent 10.2 and there was cooperation between the workman and respondent 
no.2, which involve substantial commercial element for rendering service to satisfy human wants. Thus, respondent 
no.2 would be termed as industry. 


20. Workman in his deposition has clearly stated that there was non-compliance of Section 25F, 25G and 25H of 
the Act. He also stated that he was appointed on 18.10.2016 and he was paid minimum wages prescribed by Central 
Government and was working with respondent 10.1. He was not given any compensation before terminating his 
services on 27.10.2018. In his cross examination, he has further stated that his salary used to be credited in his bank 
account. But he has not placed on record any bank account, in which his salary was credited in order to enable this 
Court to see who was making payment to the workman. However, there is no denial that the workman was paid salary 
by respondent no.2 (contractor). However, from the agreement dated 05.07.2018 (Ex.R-2) placed on file by 
respondent no.1, it emerges that safai karamcharis were provided by respondent no.2 (contractor) to work with 
respondent 10.1. Thus, workman was employee of respondent no.2 and not of respondent 10.1 as has been discussed 
above. There does not exist any relationship of employee and employer between the workman and respondent no.1. 
However, there exists relation of employee and employer between the workman and respondent 10.2. 


21. Admittedly, there is non-compliance of Section 25F of the Act by respondent no.2. However, as regards 
violation of other provisions i.e. Section 25G and 25H of the Act, there is no evidence lead by the workman. Hence, 
workman is entitled for compensation from respondent 10.2.

by entering into contract with contractors for supply of safai karamcharis and agreement executed between 
respondent 10.1 and 2 cannot be said to be any unfair labour practice. So far as contentions of AR for workman that 
the work performed by the workman is of perennial in nature and no domestic inquiry was held before terminating 
the services of workman are concerned, in this regard, it is pointed out that workman was entitled only for 
compensation under Section 25F of the Act by respondent no.2 (contractor) and no domestic inquiry was required to 
be conducted. Merely because work is of perennial in nature does not mean that any right has accrued in favour of the 
workman to get employment with respondent 10.1, which is a department of Civil Defence run by Government of 
India and for that regular recruitment procedure is provided. Workman cannot seek backdoor entry into service. 
Moreover, workman is not employee of respondent 10.1 being employee of respondent 10.2 (contractor).

respondent 10.1, so keeping in view the tenure of service rendered by the workman and salary given to him during the 
period of his stay with the contractor and non-compliance of Section 25F of the Act, this Tribunal is of the considered 
opinion that workman is entitled for compensation.

19. TheHon’ble Apex Court in the case of Banglore Water Supply & Sewerage Board Vs. A. Rajappa 1978(36) 


FLR 266 dealt at length with the ambit and scope of expression “industry” as defined in Section 2(j) of the Act, and 
has laid down triple test for determining whether a particular establishment is industry or not. The triple test is where 
(a) systematic activity (b) organized by cooperation between employer and employee (the direct and substantial 
element is commercial (c) for the production or distribution of goods and services to calculated to satisfy human 
wants and wishes prima facie is an “Industry” in that enterprise. The workman was doing work i.e. systematic activity 
for respondent 10.1 at the asking of respondent 10.2 and there was cooperation between the workman and respondent 
no.2, which involve substantial commercial element for rendering service to satisfy human wants. Thus, respondent 
no.2 would be termed as industry. 


20. Workman in his deposition has clearly stated that there was non-compliance of Section 25F, 25G and 25H of 
the Act. He also stated that he was appointed on 20.10.2016 and he was paid minimum wages prescribed by Central 
Government and was working with respondent 10.1. He was not given any compensation before terminating his 
services on 27.10.2018. In his cross examination, he has further stated that his salary used to be credited in his bank 
account. But he has not placed on record any bank account, in which his salary was credited in order to enable this 
Court to see who was making payment to the workman. However, there is no denial that the workman was paid salary 
by respondent no.2 (contractor). However, from the agreement dated 05.07.2018 (Ex.R-2) placed on file by 
respondent no.1, it emerges that safai karamcharis were provided by respondent no.2 (contractor) to work with 
respondent no.1. Thus, workman was employee of respondent no.2 and not of respondent no.1 as has been discussed 
above. There does not exist any relationship of employee and employer between the workman and respondent 10.1. 
However, there exists relation of employee and employer between the workman and respondent no.2. 


21. Admittedly, there is non-compliance of Section 25F of the Act by respondent no.2. However, as regards 
violation of other provisions i.e. Section 25G and 25H of the Act, there is no evidence lead by the workman. Hence, 
workman is entitled for compensation from respondent 10.2. 


22; It is also added here that there is no iota of evidence that any unfair labour practice used by respondent no.1 
by entering into contract with contractors for supply of safai karamcharis and agreement executed between 
respondent 10.1 and 2 cannot be said to be any unfair labour practice. So far as contentions of AR for workman that 
the work performed by the workman is of perennial in nature and no domestic inquiry was held before terminating 
the services of workman are concerned, in this regard, it is pointed out that workman was entitled only for 
compensation under Section 25F of the Act by respondent no.2 (contractor) and no domestic inquiry was required to 
be conducted. Merely because work is of perennial in nature does not mean that any right has accrued in favour of the 
workman to get employment with respondent no.1, which is a department of Civil Defence run by Government of 
India and for that regular recruitment procedure is provided. Workman cannot seek backdoor entry into service. 
Moreover, workman is not employee of respondent 10.1 being employee of respondent no.2 (contractor). 


23. In view of above discussion, it is held that since respondent no.2 (contractor) is currently not working with 
respondent 10.1, so keeping in view the tenure of service rendered by the workman and salary given to him during the 
period of his stay with the contractor and non-compliance of Section 25F of the Act, this Tribunal is of the considered 
opinion that workman is entitled for compensation. 


24. Keeping in view the fact and circumstances of the present case, the following scheme of compensation is 
deemed fit by this Tribunal: 


1. Workman who worked for less than 2 years with contractor shall be entitled for Rs.20,000/-. 

il. Workman who worked for more than 2 years but less than 5 years with contractor shall be entitled 
Rs.30,000/-. 

ili. Workman who worked for more than 5 years with contractors shall be entitled for Rs.50,000/-. 

25. Present workman employed on 20.10.2016 and was terminated on 27.10.2018 (more than 2 years and less 


than 5 years), so he is entitled for Rs.30,000/-. 


26. Respondent no.2 is directed to pay the workman Rs.30,000/- within one month from the date of the 
notification of the award failing which the respondent 10.2 shall further pay interest @6% per annum from the date of 
award till the date of making payment. It is also added here that in case respondent 10.1 requires safai karamcharis, 
then workman may be engaged through any contractor on sympathetic ground. 


27. Let copy of this award be sent to Central Government for publication as required under Section 17 of the 
Act.

has been made to this Tribunal under Section-10 of Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 (in short the ‘Act’) as per 
Notification No.L-12012/70/2015(IR(B-I1)) dt. 18/02/2016. The dispute under reference relates to:- 


“क्या आवेवक श्री अभिषेक चॉरासिया आत्मज श्री अनित्र चौरसिया दिनांक 1/9/11 से विनांक 15/2/2015 तक 
आओरियण्टन बैंक ऑफ कामर्स की शाखा छिंदवाडा में बतौर दैनिक वेतन भोगी कर्मचारी नियोजित थे, ale हां तो क्या 
शाया प्रबंधक TART आवेवक श्री अभिषेक चॉरासिया को बिना किसी पूर्व TIA HR के विनांक 16/2/15 से BAT से 
हटाना न्यायसंगत हैं? यवि नहीं तो HATH क्या अनुतोष पाने का अधिकारी हैं? " 


After registering the case on the basis of reference, notices were issued to the parties. They appeared and 
filed their respective statement of claim in defense. 


4180 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : MAY 9, 2026/VAISAKHA 19, 1948 [PART II—SEC. 3(ii)] 


The case of the workman is mainly that he was appointed as a ‘Messenger’ w.e.f. 01.09.2011 on daily rated 
basis and worked continuously with the Bank till 15.02.2015, when his services were terminated under an oral order 
without notice or compensation. According to the workman union, this action of management is in violation of 
Section 25-F and 25-G of the Act, hence unjust, illegal and arbitrary. He raised a dispute in this respect which could 
not be conciliated, hence this Reference. 


The workman has prayed that, holding termination of his service against the Act, he be held entitled to be 
reinstated with back-wages and benefits and also be held entitled to permanent status. 


Case of the Management Bank is mainly that they are a Public Sector Undertaking and have defined Rules 
for Appointment of staff, Branch Manager is not an Employer to employ any staff. The workman was never appointed 
against any permanent vacancy of Messenger following any recruitment process, there is no post of messenger as 
such in the Bank. According to the Bank, he was a daily rated worker, engaged by Bank on as and when required 
basis, for which he was paid his daily wages. He never completed 240 days in any year; management has requested 
that the reference be answered against the workman. 


In evidence, the workman has filed his affidavit as his Examination-in-chief, he has been cross-examined by 
management Bank, management Bank has also filed affidavit of its witness who has been cross-examined by 
workman side. The workman has also filed and proved Ex-W/1, certificate issued by Branch Manager and Ex-W/2 
which are 76 vouchers for the period between 2014-2015 with regard to payment made by the Bank to workman. 


I have heard argument of Learned Counsel for workman Mr. Sidharth Verma. Learned Counsel for 
management Bank did not appear for argument. Both the parties have filed written submissions which are part of the 
record. I have gone through the written submissions and record as well. 


On perusal of record in light of written submissions, following Issues came up for determination:- 


4) Whether the workman has successfully proved his continuous engagement for 240 days as 
defined under section 25-B of the Act? 

2) Whether the termination of services of workman is in violation of section 25-F & 25-G of the 
Act? 

3) Whether the workman is entitled to any relief? 

Issue No.1, 


Section 25-B of the Act, which defines ‘continuous service’, is being reproduced as follows:- 


“25B. Definition of continuous service.—For the purposes of this Chapter,— 


(1) a workman shall be said to be in continuous service for a period if he is, for that period, 
in uninterrupted service, including service which may be interrupted on account of 
sickness or authorised leave or an accident or a strike which is not illegal, or a lock-out 
or a cessation of work which is not due to any fault on the part of the workman; 


(2) where a workman is not in continuous service within the meaning of clause (1) for a 
period of one year or six months, he shall be deemed to be in continuous service under 
an employer— 


(a) for a period of one year, if the workman, during a period of twelve calendar 
months preceding the date with reference to which calculation is to be made, 
has actually worked under the employer for not less than— 


(i) one hundred and ninety days in the case of a workman employed below 
ground in a mine; and 


(ii) two hundred and forty days, in any other case; 


(b) for a period of six months, if the workman, during a period of six calendar 
months preceding the date with reference to which calculation is to be made, 
has actually worked under the employer for not less than— 


(i) ninety-five days, in the case of a workman employed below ground in a 
mine; and 
(ii) one hundred and twenty days, in any other case.” 


Pleadings of the parties on this issue have been corroborated earlier. The workman has corroborated his 
allegations on this issue in his affidavit as his Examination-in-chief. In his cross-examination he admits that no 
appointment letter was issued to him, and he did not appear in any written or oral examination. He has denied that he 
did not complete 240 days in a year. 


[भाग 1---खण्ड 3(1)] भारत का राजपत्र : मई 9, 2026/वैशाख 19, 1948 4181 


On the other hand, the management witness admits in his cross-examination that he was not posted during 
the period in which the workman has claimed to have been employed by the Bank. He also states that there is no 
record with respect to payment of daily wagers in the Bank and that there is a post of Peon in the Branch but it is not 
known who was working on the post of Peon in the said period. The evidence of the workman is corroborated by 
different vouchers, total 76 in numbers which showed that he was engaged by the Bank for different works for which 
he was paid his wages and his expenses with regard to travelling, etc. These vouchers are for the period 2014-2015. 


The statement of workman is corroborated by documentary evidence. On the other hand, the statement of 
management itself shows that this witness was not posted in the Branch during the period in question. Hence, holding 
the evidence from workman side more reliable, he is held to have proved his case that he worked continuously for 240 
days and more in every year including the year preceding the date of his termination as defined under section 25-B of 
the Act and the Bank is held to be his employer under the Act. 


Issue No. 1 is answered accordingly. 
Issue No. 2, 


Undisputedly, no notice was issued to the workman before his termination nor was he paid any 
compensation. Hence his termination is held in violation of section 25-F and 25-G of the Act. 


Section 25-F & 25-G of the Act, is being reproduced as follows: 
25F. Conditions precedent to retrenchment of workmen. 


No workman employed in any industry who has been in continuous service for not less than one 
year under an employer shall be retrenched by that employer until- 


(a) the workman has been given one month's notice in writing indicating the reasons for 
retrenchment and the period of notice has expired, or the workman has been paid in lieu 
of such notice, wages for the period of the notice; 


(b) the workman has been paid, at the time of retrenchment, compensation which shall be 
equivalent to fifteen days' average pay for every completed year of continuous service or 
any part thereof in excess of six months; and 


(c) notice in the prescribed manner is served on the appropriate Government or such 
authority as may be specified by the appropriate Government by notification in the 
Official Gazette. 


25G ‘Procedure _for_retrenchment.—Where any workman in an industrial establishment, who is a 
citizen of India, is to be retrenched and he belongs to a particular category of workmen in that 
establishment, in the absence of any agreement between the employer and the workman in this 
behalf, the employer shall ordinarily retrench the workman who was the last person to be 
employed in that category, unless for reasons to be recorded the employer retrenches any other 
workman. 


Issue No. 2 stands answered accordingly. 
Issue No. 3 


Undisputedly, the workman was not appointed following recruitment process hence, his engagement cannot 
be said to be legal. Thus, he is not entitled to reinstatement. Keeping in view, the facts and circumstances of the case 
in hand, a lump sum compensation quantified Rs. 1Lac/- in lieu of all his claims including litigation cost will meet the 
ends of justice which the workman is held entitled to be paid by the Bank within 60 days from the date of publication 
of the Award, failing which interest @ 6% p.a. from the date of award till payment. 

Issue No. 3 stands answered accordingly. 


In light of above discussion and findings, the reference is answered as follows.- 
AWARD 


“Holding the action of the management in disengaging the workman Shri Abhishek Chourasia from 
16/02/2015, illegal and unjustified, he is held entitled to a lump sum amount of Rs. 1Lac/- to be paid by the Bank 
within 60 days from the date of publication Award, failing which interest @ 6% p.a. from the date of award till 
payment, in lieu of all his claims.” 


No order as to cost.

AWARD 


The present reference has been made by the Central Government by its order No. L-30012/23/2017-IR(M) 
dated 17/05/2018 passed in exercise of the powers conferred by clause (d) of section (1) read with sub-section (2A) of 
Section 10 of the Industrial Dispute Act 1947. The terms of reference as per the schedule to the said order are as 
under: 


“Whether the action of the management of Indian Oil Corporation Limited through its General Manager 
(Regional Services)-WR, IOCL, Mumbai in dismissing the workman namely Sh. Jeery Teles, Jr. Operator (F), 
Aviation Fuel Station, Nagpur vide order bearing No. WR.IR/1461/JT dated 08/09/2006 is legal & proper? If 
not, what relief to the workman is entitled to?” 


In view of the above said facts the claimant/workman has not field evidence in support of his case on affidavit, in 
spite of several opportunities given to him and taking into consideration the law as laid by the Hon'ble High Court in 
the case of V. K. Raj Industries v. Labour Court (1) and others 1981 (29) FLR 194 as under: 


“It is well settled that if a party challenges the legality of an order, the burden lies upon him to prove illegality 
of the order and if no evidence is produced the party invoking jurisdiction of the Court must fail. Whenever a 
workman raises a dispute challenging the validity of the termination of service if is imperative for him to file 
written statement before the Industrial Court setting out grounds on which the order is challenged and he must 
also produce evidence to prove his case. If the workman fails to appear or to file written statement or produce 
evidence, the dispute referred by the State Government cannot be answered in favour of the workman and he 
would not be entitled to any relief.” 


[भाग 1---खण्ड 3(1)] भारत का राजपत्र : मई 9, 2026/वैशाख 19, 1948 4183 


In the case of M/s Uptron Powertronics Employees’ Union, Ghaziabad through its Secretary v. Presiding Officer, 
Labour Court (II), Ghaziabad and others 2008 (118) FLR 1164 Hon’ble Allahabad High Court has held as under: 


“The law has been settled by the Apex Court in case of Shanker Chakravarti v. Britannia Biscuit Co. Ltd., V.K. 
Raj Industries v. Labour Court and Ors., Airtech Private Limited v. State of U.P. and Ors. 1984 (49) FLR 38 
and Meritech India Ltd. v. State of U.P. and Ors. 1996 FLR that in the absence of any evidence led by or on 
behalf of the workman the reference is bound to be answered by the court against the workman. In such a 
situation it is not necessary for the employers to lead any evidence at all. The obligation to lead evidence to 
establish an allegation made by a party is on the party making the allegation. The test would be, who would fail 
if no evidence is led.” 


And by the Hon’ble Allahabad High Court in the case of District Administrative Committee, U.P. P.A.C.C.S.C. 
Services v. Secretary-cum-G.M. District Co-operative Bank Ltd. 2010 (126) FLR 519; wherein it has been held as 
under: 


“The submission is that even if the petitioner failed to lead the evidence, burden was on the shoulders of the 
respondent to prove the termination order as illegal. He was required to lead evidence first which he failed. A 
perusal of the impugned award also does not show that any evidence either oral or documentary was led by the 
respondent. In the case of no evidence, the reference has to be dismissed.” 


Mr. S.V. Alva, Learned Counsel for the Management, appeared and he prayed that the matter be dismissed for want 
of prosecution. 


Since claimant/workman has not field evidence in support of his case on affidavit, in spite of several opportunities 
given to him, the claim is liable to be dismissed. 


For the foregoing reasons, the case is dismissed and the workman is not entitled for any relief. 
Accordingly, the reference stands answered in terms aforesaid. 
Award as above.

situation it is not necessary for the employers to lead any evidence at all. The obligation to lead evidence to 
establish an allegation made by a party is on the party making the allegation. The test would be, who would 
fail if no evidence is led.” 


And by the Hon’ble Allahabad High Court in the case of District Administrative Committee, U.P. P.A.C.C.S.C. 
Services v. Secretary-cum-G.M. District Co-operative Bank Ltd. 2010 (126) FLR 519; wherein it has been held as 
under: 


“The submission is that even if the petitioner failed to lead the evidence, burden was on the shoulders of the 
respondent to prove the termination order as illegal. He was required to lead evidence first which he failed. A 
perusal of the impugned award also does not show that any evidence either oral or documentary was led by the 
respondent. In the case of no evidence, the reference has to be dismissed.”

ISSUE NO. वा 


10. At the outset of discussions, it is relevant to mention here that it is an admitted fact that the concerned 
workman namely Sri Nilamani Sahu had been appointed as Chowkidar after selection through interview against the 
permanent vacancy with effect from 01.06.1985 at Bhubaneswar and after completion of probation his service was

and liberty of a superior officer in jeopardy and as such deserves no lenient view from the Management. It has also

14. It is relevant to mention herewith that there is a Standing Order for the workmen employed in the 
establishment of Oil India Limited which is marked as Ext.-16. The Management had not raised any objection at 
the time of its marking as exhibit by the W.W.-2 (Sri N.R. Mallick). Since no objection had been raised by the 
Management on the copy of the Standing Order for the workman employed in the establishment of Oil India Limited 
(Ext.-16), so it amounts to admission on the part of the Management. 


15. In the Standing Order the provisions of termination of employment/service has been mentioned under 
Section 19 which reads as follows:- 


19.0. Termination of Employment/Service :- 


19.1. | Reasons :- 

19.1.1 A workman’s termination of service will generally fall under one of the following categories:- 
(a) Discharge owing to staff redundancy. 
(b) Discharge on completion of temporary work. 


(c) Discharge on completion of probationary period in respect of new recruits (Gf work is found 
unsatisfactory during the probationary period.

(h) Discharge on attainment of age of superannuation.

(j) Discharge for unsatisfactory service.

21. In absence of the copy of the registration of Police Case and copy of the charge-sheet submitted by Police on 
the I.C.C. case filed by Sri Mazumdar the case of the Management regarding incident on 13.06.2006 does not seem to 
be probable and trust-worthy. 


22. After analysing the evidence of both the parties it is crystal clear that the concerned workman namely Sri 
Nilamani Sahoo had been dismissed from _ service of the Management without holding any departmental enquiry 
which is in violation of the Standing Order of the management of Oil India Limited (Ext.-16). 


23. In view of such, the action of the management in dismissing/terminating the services of concerned workman 
w.e.f. 30.06.2010 is not legal and justified. Hence the concerned workman is entitled for relief. 


Accordingly, the Issue No. I is answered in favour of the 2™ Party- Workman.

9. The most important issue in this case is Issue No. I, so the Tribunal thinks it proper to discuss this issue first

ISSUE NO. I 
10. At the outset of discussions, it is relevant to mention here that it is an admitted fact that the concerned 


workman namely Sri T. Narayan had been appointed as Photocopier Operator after selection through interview 
against the permanent vacancy with effect from 01.06.1985 at Bhubaneswar and after completion of probation his 
service was confirmed. 


4196 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : MAY 9, 2026/VAISAKHA 19, 1948 [PART II—SEC. 3(ii)] 


11. It is also the admitted fact that the concerned workman namely Sri T. Narayan had been dismissed/removed 
from the services with effect from 30.06.2006 without holding any domestic enquiry against him for the alleged 
misconduct. 


12. At this stage it is required to mention here that in the dismissal order of Sri T. Narayan which is at Ext.-3, it 
has been mentioned that the misconduct committed by him is grave and serious in nature putting the life and liberty of 
a superior officer in jeopardy and as such deserves no lenient view from the Management. It has also been mentioned 
that he had taken extreme step of using abusive language and assaulting Sri Mazumdar inside the office premises 
in presence of other employees and such act in itself speaks of his high handed and recalcitrant attitude. It has been 
further noted that the Management is of view that it would be difficult to hold a proper enquiry since the witness 
might not come forward to give frank and true evidence. 


13. It is relevant to mention herewith that there is a Standing Order for the workmen employed in the 
establishment of Oil India Limited which is marked as Ext.-16. The Management had not raised any objection at the 
time of its marking as exhibit by the W.W.-2 (Sri N.R. Mallick). Since no objection had been raised by the 
Management on the copy of the Standing Order for the workman employed in the establishment of Oil India Limited 
(Ext.-16), so it amounts to admission on the part of the Management. 


14. In the Standing Order the provisions of termination of employment/service has been mentioned under 
Section 19 which reads as follows:- 


19.0. Termination of Employment/Service :- 


19.1. | Reasons :- 

19.1.1 A workman’s termination of service will generally fall under one of the following categories: - 
(a) Discharge owing to staff redundancy. 
(b) Discharge on completion of temporary work. 


(c) Discharge on completion of probationary period in respect of new recruits (if work is found 
unsatisfactory during the probationary _ period. 


(d) Discharge on receipt of adverse report about the workman’s efficiency, work, acts or expression 
prejudicial to the company, its management, its business or acts or expression prejudicial to the company, its 
management, its business or its reputation or any adverse official report. 


(e) Discharge for absence from work, without authorized leave or permission for more than fourteen 
consecutive days. 


(f) Any discharge for any misstatement or suppression of facts or furnishing to the Company any false or 
incorrect particulars about himself/herself/family, his/her qualifications or experience or past antecedents or 
conduct at the time of the appointment. 


(g) Discharge or conviction by any Court of Law for a criminal offence involving moral turpitude. 
(h) Discharge on attainment of age of superannuation. 

(i) Discharge on resignation after due notice. 

(j) Discharge for unsatisfactory service. 

(k) Dismissal for any act of misconduct as specified under Section 21. 

Clause (a) to (k) 


Further, Section-19.2 of the Standing Order mentions the procedure for termination of 
employment/service and under Section-19.2.(d) it has been specifically mentioned that the services of the 
workman shall not be terminated (dismissed) for an act of misconduct specified under section 21 of the Standing 
Orders unless he/she has been given an opportunity to explain the charges levelled against him/her and a 
departmental enquiry is held. Further, under section 21 of the Standing Order disciplinary action of misconduct has 
been mentioned. 


15. Now in the Standing Order of the Management of Oil India Limited __ there is categorical provision that a 
workman shall not be terminated (dismissed) for an act of misconduct unless he has been given an opportunity to 
explain and after holding a departmental enquiry. But in this case the Management had not issued any 
explanation/show cause to the concern workman with regard to his misconduct as mentioned in the dismissal 
order and no disciplinary enquiry was conducted against him for proving the charges of misconduct. 


16. However, at this stage the Tribunal thinks it proper to discuss the oral and documentary evidence of both the 
parties even though no departmental enquiry was conducted against the workman.

Petitioner had filed Writ petition number 27455 of 2012 before the Hon’ble High Court of Andhra Pradesh, 
questioning transfer order issued by the Respondent, transferring him from Hyderabad to Rajahmundry and Hon’ble 
High Court decline to grant any interim relief, Writ Petition, was withdrawn and High Court dismissed the Writ 
Petition as withdrawn. Therefore, Respondent prayed to dismiss the claim statement of the Petitioner. 


4. In support of averment made in the claim statement, Petitioner has filed chief statement affidavit of WW1, 
Respondent has also filed chief statement affidavit of MW1. Petitioner has also filed certain photocopies of the 
documents. 


[भाग 1---खण्ड 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : मई 9, 2026/वैशाख 19, 1948 4205 
on the basis of pleadings of either parties following issues arise for determination in this 2856:- 


I. Whether the action of Management of Airport Authority of India, Hyderabad, in connection with the transfer of 
workman Sri Mohd Ghouse, Senior Assistant, Lift and Bench Secretary of Airport Authority of India Workers Union, 
Hyderabad, from Hyderabad to Rajahmundry, is legal and justified? 


II. To what relief, if any, Petitioner is entitled to? 
Findings:- 
ISSUE No. I:- 


Petitioner in his claim statement has challenged transfer order dated 23.08.2012, from Hyderabad to 
Rajahmundry Airport, on the ground of unfair labour practices, victimization and change in service condition in 
violation of provision contained u/s 9 A of the ID. Act. 


At the outset, learned counsel for Respondent has contended that Petitioner-workman, whose dispute has 
been referred has attained the age of superannuation on 30.06.2014, and has settled all his claims. Therefore, present 
reference has become infructuous for the reason as no cause of action survives on account of his retirement, and no 
relief can be granted to the Petitioner. The contention of Respondent that Petitioner-workman has got retired after the 
age of superannuation on 30.06.2014, is not controverted and denied by the Petitioner in his oral testimony. 
Therefore, it is undisputed that Petitioner got retired from service at the age of superannuation on 30.06.2014 and has 
settled all his claims. It is not the case of the Petitioner that due to his transfer from Airport Hyderabad he has suffered 
financial disadvantages. It is settled law that where an employee challenging his transfer order in a labor Court 
subsequently retires during the pendency of the case, the relief sought specifically the cancellation of the transfer 
order and related service benefits during the contested period, may become infructuous or difficult to grant due to the 
cessation of the employment relationship. The primary remedy, reinstatement to the original post, is generally not 
possible after a valid retirement. Therefore, upon retirement of an employee, the employer-employee relationship 
ceases and main remedies of service law, like setting aside a transfer, preventing termination, are generally 
prospective and tied to active service. Therefore, this court cannot typically order the employee to be placed in a 
specific active-duty post or reverse the effect of the past transfer order as if the employee was still in service. The 
claim for the primary relief becomes obsolete. Therefore, in view of the above, in the present matter Petitioner has 
already retired from his post after attaining the age of superannuation on 30.06.2014. Thus, the relief claimed by the 
Petitioner for conciliation of his transfer order has become infructuous and same is not maintainable. 


Now, let us examine legality of impugned transfer order of Petitioner from Hyderabad to Rajahmundry. In 
this context, Petitioner has filed a chief affidavit of statement of WW1, wherein he has reiterated the averment made 
in claim petition. But in cross-examination WW1 has stated that it is true that he has not marked any exhibit in 
support of his claim in his chief examination affidavit. It is true that he was relieved on 31.08.2012, by a transfer 
order issued by the Respondent. Further, WW1 states that it is true that he has filed writ petition number 27455 of 
2012, and same was dismissed as withdrawn. Further, WW1 states that it is true that he has not filed any document to 
show that his transfer from Hyderabad to Rajahmundry was to accommodate one Mr. Srinivas, office assistant. It is 
true that he has not filed any documents to show that he cannot be transferred from Begumpet, Hyderabad, to any 
other place. Thus, from the above statement of witness WW1, it manifests that Petitioner has utterly failed to prove 
the averment made in his claim statement that he was posted on a non-transferable post and he has been transfers from 
Hyderabad to Rajahmundry on the ground victimization and unfair labour practice and also in violation of Section 9 
A of Industrial Dispute Act. Further, Petitioner has failed to prove the fact the due to impugned transfer order how his 
service condition has been changed. 


Whereas, Respondent has filed an affidavit of examination-in-chief statement of MW1 in oral evidence and 
therein MW1 has stated that, according to Ministry of Civil Aviation Airport Authority of India order number 2002, 
liability for service is transferable anywhere in India or abroad. Further, MW1 has deposed that the employees of the 
Begumpet airport had been redeployed by transferring them to other places so that their services could be gainfully 
utilized at some other places without altering their service conditions, and this is not in violation of section 9A of the 
Industrial Disputes Act. Further, MW1 states that the Begumpet airport of Hyderabad was closed for commercial 
aircraft operation, and it was shifted to Shamshabad airport, as per a Central Government notification dated 
10.03.2008. Further, MW1 stated that both the terminal buildings, 1.6., NTR terminal building and Rajiv Gandhi 
terminal building, were not operated as there were no commercial passenger movements from Begumpet airport. 
Therefore, the escalator and lift in those terminal buildings were not functioning for passenger facilities. Hence, the 
workman-Petitioner was transferred from Hyderabad to Rajahmundry airport by order dated 23.08.2012, and other 
workmen were also transferred to other places, and Petitioner was relieved from his duty. Further, MW1 stated that 
the other employees reported for duty at the transferred places, but the workman-Petitioner failed to report for duty at 
the transferred place. 


Thus, witness MW1 in his chief statement has proved that Petitioner was transferred from Begumpet airport 
to Shamshabad airport due to close of Commercial Aircraft operation at airport Begumpet. Further, MW1 has proved 
that terminal buildings of the Begumpet airport were not in operation as there was no commercial passenger 


4206 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : MAY 9, 2026/VAISAKHA 19, 1948 [PART II—SEC. 3(ii)] 


movement at Begumpet airport and due to non-availability of work at Begumpet airport, the employees including 
Petitioner deputed at Begumpet Airport were transferred to other places by the Respondent Management. Thus, it 
reflects from the testimony of MW1 that the Petitioner was transferred to Rajahmundry Airport by the Respondent 
Management due to administrative reasons. Moreover, Petitioner failed to produce any document to prove his 
averment that his service was non-transferable, and he was transferred from Begumpet Airport due to victimization. 
Moreover, despite sufficient opportunity, Petitioner failed to cross-examine witness MW1. Therefore, statement of 
witness MW1 in the chief statement affidavit remained uncontroverted. 


In this context, reference of decision of Hon’ble Supreme Court in the case of Mrs. Shilpi Bose and 
Others Vs State of Bihar, A.LR., 1991 Supreme Court, page 532, is relevant wherein Hon’ble Supreme Court: - 


“In our opinion, the Courts should not interfere with a transfer Order which are made in public interest and 
for administrative reasons unless the transfer Orders are made in violation of any mandatory statutory Rule or on the 
ground of malafide. A Government Servant holding a transferable post has no vested right to remain posted at one 
place or the other, he is hable to be transferred from one place to other. Transfer Orders issued by the competent 
authority do not violate any of his legal rights. Even if a transfer Order is passed in violation of exceptive instructions 
or orders, the courts ordinarily should not interfere with the order instead affected party should approach the higher 
authorities in the Department. If the Courts continue to interfere with day-to-day transfer orders issued by the 
Government and its subordinate authorities, there will be complete chaos in the administration which would not be 
conducive to public interest. The High court overlooked these aspects in interfering with the transfer orders.” 


Further, Hon’ble Supreme Court ion the case of State of Madhya Pradesh Vs. S.S. Kaurav 1995A.1LR., page 1056, 
have held: - 


“It is contended for the respondent that the respondent had already worked at Jagdalpur from 1982 to 1989 
and when he was transferred to Bhopal, there was no justification to retransfer him again to Jagdalpur. We cannot 
appreciate these grounds/The courts or Tribunals are not appellate forums to decide on transfers of officers on 
administrative grounds. The wheels of administration should be allowed to run smoothly and the courts or tribunals 
are not expected to interdict the working of the administrative system by transferring the officers to proper places. It 
is for the administration to take appropriate decision and such decisions shall stand unless they are vitiated either by 
malafides or by extraneous consideration without any factual background foundation. In this case we have seen that 
on the administrative grounds the transfer orders came to be issued. Therefore, we cannot go into the expediency of 
posting an officer at a particular place" 


Thus, in view of the law laid down by Apex Court as discussed above and ongoing evidence material on 
record in the matter at hand the Petitioner was transferred by Respondent Management from Begumpet Airport to 
Rajahmundry Airport due to stoppage of operation of commercial passenger flight and there was no work available 
for the employees posted at Begumpet Airport. Since Petitioner was posted at Begumpet Airport as escalator and lift 
operator which were closed due to shift of commercial passenger flight from Begumpet to Shamshabad. Therefore, 
the Petitioner and other employees were transferred from Begumpet Airport purely on the administrative ground. 
Therefore, the impugned order of transfer of Petitioner under challenge in this Petition warrants no interference by the 
tribunal and Petition filed by the Petitioner sans merit hence liable to dismissed. 


Further, as regard other pleas of the Petitioner taken in the claim statement regarding withdrawal of overtime 
and other benefits it would be pertinent to mention here that the said pleas raised by Petitioner in his claim statement 
are outside the scope of reference in this case and need not to be discussed and answered here. It is settled law that the 
jurisdiction of the Labour Court/Tribunal is limited to the points specifically referred and matter incidental thereto. 
Since the scope of its jurisdiction and power of the tribunal is circumscribed by the order of reference, it is not 
permissible for it to go beyond the term of the reference. Therefore, the issue is decided against the petitioner. 


ISSUE NO. II: - 


In view of discussion and finding given at ISSUE No. I, Petitioner claim statement sans merit and liable to be 
dismissed. Petitioner is not entitled to any relief. 


AWARD 


The action of management of Airport Authority of India, Hyderabad, in connection with the transfer of workman, 
Shri Mohd Gouse Senior, Senior Assistant Lift and Branch Secretary Airport Authority of India Worker Union, 
Hyderabad, from Hyderabad to Rajahmundry is held legal and justified. Petitioners claim statement sans merit hence 
dismissed. The reference is answered accordingly. 


Award is passed accordingly. Transmit.

paid to them by the dealers of different Oil companies are far below the prescribed rate of wages as availed by other 
contract labourers of Oil India Ltd., Indian Oil Corporation, Oil and Natural Gas Corporation Limited etc. It is 
submitted that in course of carrying of petroleum products including Gases, the workers have to face different 
situation such as high jack of vehicle and killing of drivers or handyman and in such situation the legal heirs of those 
employees do not even get financial help to maintain their liveli hood. It is further stated that when petroleum 
products are loaded at the concerned loading centre, the tanker remains locked and the concerned key is kept in the 
loading centre itself and the transporter carries petroleum products from the loading centre and delivers the same at 
the concerned petrol pump, in which process, the employees have no control over the quality or quantity of the 
petroleum products carried through the tankers. It is stated that when a tanker reached the petrol pump, it is unlocked 
through a master key kept in the petrol pump. But if it is found that there is shortage in the quantity of the Petroleum

strike dated 15-06-2020 issued by APMU was uncalled and demands made thereunder was not tenable in law. In this

Sri Ramen Das, the General Secretary, Assam Petroleum Mazdoor Union, Guwahati filed his evidence on

Workmen witness-2 Sri Nipen Das working as the petrol pump operator in Nava Service Station, Zoo Road,

In this case, the workmen/Union submitted evidence on affidavit of five witnesses in support of their claim 
statement but lateron they failed to appear for cross examination. Record reveals that the case is pending for cross 
examination of workmen witnesses since 25-09-2019, and since 20-10-2022 the workmen remained absent without 
any step. Even on receipt of fresh notice on 01-01-2026, the workmen did not appear today i.e. on 05-02-2026 when

witnesses did not turn up for cross examination. Hence their evidence, can not be considered in deciding the dispute 
in issue.

be ordered even when the enquiry was earlier conducted. The workman side could not refer any judgment laying a 
proposition of law that a second enquiry or a fresh enquiry cannot be ordered even during pendency of first enquiry. 
Hence, the argument from the workman side that the second enquiry itself is against law and malafide cannot be 
accepted. The workman side could not point any defect with respect to substance or procedure in form of any 
illegality or material irregularity in conducting the enquiry. The charges are acts of moral turpitude hence, major 
punishment of dismissal cannot be held to be disproportionate to the charges proved. 


In light of above discussion and findings, the reference is answered as follows.- 
AWARD 


“Holding the action of the management of Union Bank of India, to terminate the services of the workman 
Shri Gopal Singh Chauhan, justified, the workman is held entitled to no relief.” 


No order as to cost.

1.Workman has filed the present claim petition under Section 2A of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 
(hereinafter called the Act) against his termination w.e.f. 27.10.2018 claiming reinstatement into service along 
with continuity of service and full back wages. 


2.It is maintained by the workman in the claim petition that that he was appointed as sweeper/safai karamchari 
on 01.06.2013 by respondent 10.1 at minimum wages prescribed by the Central Government. But the said 


[भाग 1---खण्ड 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : मई 9, 2026/वैशाख 19, 1948 4227 


minimum wages were never paid to him. Management has unlawfully deducted 12% EPF share, 1.75% ESI 
and Rs.300/- as TDS from his salary despite of the fact that his total wages comes under the ambit of tax free 
limit. He was working under respondent 10.1 directly, but respondent 10.1 in order to avoid its liability always 
shows his employment in record under different contractors, which tantamount to unfair labour practice. 


3.It is further maintained that workman including 200 other safai karamcharis of respondent 10.1 raised the 
demand for non-deduction of TDS from the wages paid by respondent no.1. However, their demand was not 
accepted. Other workers working under respondent 10.1 formed union and subsequently his services were 
dispensed with w.e.f. 27.10.2018. It is also maintained that respondent 10.1 retained juniors in service and also 
made fresh appointments after termination of his services and no compensation was paid under Section 25F of 
the Act. Thus, there is violation of Section 25F, 25G and 25H of the Act. Hence this petition. 


4.Notice of the petition was given to respondents. 


5.Respondent 10.1 filed reply to the claim petition maintaining therein that the workman has not come to the 
Court with clean hands as he was appointed as sweeper by respondent no.2 (contractor) at minimum wage rate 
as prescribed by the Central Government. As per Government Policy dated 18.03.2011 (Ex.R-1), Non- 
Cantonment Military Stations have been authorized to outsource conservancy safaiwala. The answering 
respondent entered into contract with various private agencies for outsourcing of sweepers (safai karamcharis). 
In July 2018, the answering respondent entered into contract with M/s AA Foundation for safety and M/s 
Sunrise Facilitator Pvt. Ltd. through e-tendering for outsourcing of safai karamcharis to provide conservancy 
services in Chandi Mandir Military Station for the financial year 2018-19. Respondent no.2 submits bill for 
payment for the days the safai karamcharis performed their duties and answering respondent is only 
responsible to forward these bills to PCDA Western Command Chandigarh to release payment directly to the 
contractor’s account. Salary is paid to the workman by the contractor. Compliance of PF, ESI Rules etc. is 
carried out by the contractor as per contract agreement. Answering respondent has no responsibility of 
disbursement of wages and deduction of EPF and ESI etc. The workman and other safai karamcharis formed 
union in the headquarter, which is not permitted and also carried out demonstration inside the premises of 
Station Headquarter on 27.10.2018 and failed to perform his duties. Thereafter, answering respondent asked 
respondent no.2 to ask the workers to perform their duties. Answering respondent has no role or responsibility 
for termination services of the workman. There is no relationship of employer and employee between the 
answering respondent and the workman. In view of Army Headquarter Letter, the civilian employees of the 
answering respondent cannot organize themselves into trade unions as station headquarter is an administrative 
office of the Government of India. In spite of that, workman along with other safai karamcharis formed union 
unauthorizedly and indulge in unlawful activities. It is maintained that workman is the employee of contractor 
and therefore, termination is the prerogative of the contractor. It is prayed that the claim be dismissed. 


6.Respondent 10.2 also filed reply maintaining therein that workman worked with it w.e.f. 05.07.2018 to 
27.10.2018. Respondent no.2 has not terminated the services of workman. Workman was paid minimum 
wages as declared by the Centre Government from time to time. Workman himself left the job at his own will 
without notice. It is prayed that the claim may be dismissed. 


Evidence of workman:- 


7.In order to prove his case, workman examined himself as WW1 and tendered into evidence his affidavit 
WW I/A and has been cross examined by the AR for respondent 10.1. AR for workman closed the evidence on 
08.10.2024. 


Evidence of respondent no.1:- 


8.Respondent 10.1 examined Colonel K P Singh S/o Late Colonel P. P. Singh, OIC, Civic Cell, Station Head 
Quarter, Chandi Mandir Panchkula as MW1, who tendered into evidence his affidavit Ex.MW1/A along with 
documents Ex.R1 to Ex.R4. AR for respondent 10.1 closed the evidence on 29.01.2026.

2 Agreement with respondent no.2 05.07.2018 Ex.R-2 
33 Copy of ECR of EPFO Ex.R-3 
4 Letter of Head Quarter 22.04.1980 Ex.R-4 


9.It is pertinent to mention here that respondent no.2 was proceeded ex parte on 20.04.2023.
